subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Kenya: Africa's Tea Giant
description: Learn Kenya: Africa's Tea Giant in one minute.

hook.text: Kenya is the world's largest exporter of black tea. It exports more than India despite growing far less.

buildup.text: Kenyan tea grows at high altitude near the equator—strong sun and cool nights create bold, bright cups.

discovery.text: Most Kenyan tea is CTC (crush-tear-curl), designed for tea bags and strong brews that work well with milk.

twist.text: A small but growing specialty sector now makes hand-rolled purple tea—a unique Kenyan innovation.

climax.text: Tea supports over 3 million Kenyan livelihoods. Small farmers, not large estates, produce most of it.

punchline.text: Africa's quiet tea powerhouse, feeding the world's teapots.

quiz.question: What is unique about Kenyan purple tea?
options: It's a hand-rolled specialty tea—a Kenyan innovation

details.summary: Kenya is the world's largest tea exporter, producing over 500,000 tonnes annually from highland plantations above 1,500 meters. Almost all Kenyan tea is CTC black tea destined for tea bags and blends. Its bright, brisk liquor makes it a crucial ingredient in tea blends worldwide.
details.whyItMatters: Kenya illustrates how tea has become a global crop far beyond its Asian origins. African tea production now rivals traditional giants India and China in export volume.
takeaways: Kenya is the world's largest tea exporter by volume
Most production is CTC black tea for blends and tea bags
Highland growing above 1,500 meters produces bright, brisk tea

faq.question: Why is Kenyan tea used in so many blends?
faq.answer: Kenyan CTC tea produces a bright, coppery liquor with strong color and brisk flavor, qualities that blend well with milder teas. Its consistency and volume make it reliable for large-scale blenders. Many English and Irish breakfast teas contain a significant Kenyan component.

faq.question: Does Kenya produce any specialty teas?
faq.answer: Yes, though in small quantities. Some estates make hand-crafted purple tea from a cultivar rich in anthocyanins. White and green teas are also produced experimentally. Kenya's tea research institute has developed unique cultivars suited to African growing conditions.
